title: The Exercises
hookLine: a month-long retreat in four weeks, guided by a director

lines: A BOOK NOT MEANT TO BE READ.
cards: Here is a strange kind of book. Its author didn't write it for you to read. It's thin, full of numbered notes, lists and instructions for what to do next.
Read straight through, it can feel like the rules of a sport you've never played. That's because it isn't a book to read. It's a book to use, by one person guiding another.
The author was a Spanish soldier turned pilgrim named Ignatius of Loyola, and the friends who gathered around him became the Jesuits, the new family on this path. The book is where they start.

teach.h: WALKING AND RUNNING TRAIN THE BODY.
teach.b: Back on day two hundred thirty-seven, the examen came out of this same book. The Spiritual Exercises begin by explaining the name.

Ignatius says: just as walking, marching and running are exercises for the body, so these are exercises for the soul, ways of preparing it to let go of disordered attachments, and then to seek and find what God wants for a life.
Exercise, not information. You don't get fit reading about push-ups.

The full retreat lasts about a month, kept in quiet, and it's divided into four parts Ignatius calls weeks. They aren't calendar weeks. They're stages, and a person may spend longer in one than another.
In the first, the retreatant faces their own failures and God's mercy. In the second, they walk with Christ through his life. In the third, through his passion.
In the fourth, they stay with the risen Christ. And no one makes this alone.
The book is written for a director, a guide who meets the retreatant each day, offers the next exercise, listens, and adjusts.

teach.h: OR IN DAILY LIFE, LITTLE BY LITTLE.
teach.b: Ignatius even allows the Exercises to be made in daily life, a little each day over a longer time, for someone who can't leave home for a month. Jesus does something like it with his friends.

teach.h: COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE.
teach.b: After a busy mission, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." Apart, so you can hear.

how: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises at Jesuit and other retreat houses, either in a silent retreat of about a month with a director or in shorter adaptations; some make them in daily life over several months, meeting a director regularly.

o: Ignatius's handbook for a guided retreat
a daily prayer book to read cover to cover
a set of rules for Jesuit physical training

games.q: you want to make the Exercises, but you have a job and children, and a month away is impossible. what does Ignatius allow?
o: nothing: it's a month away or not at all.
making them in daily life, a little each day over a longer time.
reading the book alone in one weekend.
games.why: Ignatius himself allows the Exercises to be made in daily life, with a director, over a longer stretch.

practice: Look at the weeks ahead and find one day, or half a day, or even two free hours, you could set apart.
Picture where you'd go, a park bench, a church, a quiet room with the phone in a drawer, and who might be your guide afterward, a friend or a priest. If you pray, offer that day ahead of time.

wordCard.voice: Spiritual Exercises. Ignatius's handbook for a guided retreat in four stages he calls weeks: training for the soul, the way walking and running train the body. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: spiritual exercises, the title of Ignatius's book.

carryVoice: Your line: exercises for the soul. Like any training, they need time set aside and someone in your corner. That's today, done.

sources.q: Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little.
